Kullback-Leibler divergence of a weighted sample from a reference sample

Source: R/calc_kl_divergence.R
calc_kl_divergence.Rd

Computes KL(P || Q), how far the distribution P of samples1 (weighted by weights1) has moved from the reference distribution Q of samples2 (weighted by weights2), in nats. In MOSAIC, P is a parameter's posterior and Q its prior, both represented by draws. The estimate is made on Q's own percentile scale, so it does not depend on the parameter's units, on heavy prior tails, on integer values or on bounds.

Usage

calc_kl_divergence(
  samples1,
  weights1 = NULL,
  samples2,
  weights2 = NULL,
  n_points = 1000,
  eps = 1e-10,
  n_bins = 20L,
  seed = 1L
)

calculate_kl_divergence(
  samples1,
  weights1 = NULL,
  samples2,
  weights2 = NULL,
  n_points = 1000,
  eps = 1e-10
)

Arguments

samples1

Numeric vector of samples from P (e.g. the posterior).

weights1

Non-negative weights for samples1, same length. If NULL, uniform weights are used.

samples2

Numeric vector of samples from Q (e.g. the prior).

weights2

Non-negative weights for samples2, same length. If NULL, uniform weights are used.

n_points

Ignored since MOSAIC 1.4.0 (kept so existing calls work; a warning is issued when supplied).

eps

Ignored since MOSAIC 1.4.0 (as n_points).

n_bins

Number of equal-probability bins on Q's percentile scale. Default 20.

seed

Integer seed of the random tie-breaking. The caller's RNG stream is restored afterwards. Default 1.

Value

A non-negative numeric value, at most log(n_bins): about 0 when P equals Q. NA with a warning when the Kish effective sample size of weights1 is below n_bins; 0 with a warning when all samples are equal.

Details

Percentile-scale (PIT) estimator. Each draw of P is mapped to its percentile under Q, \(u = F_Q(x)\). Under Q itself \(u\) is uniform, so the KL divergence is unchanged by this monotone map and becomes the divergence of the distribution of \(u\) from U(0, 1). The unit interval is cut into \(B\) = n_bins equal bins, \(p_b\) is the P-weight in bin \(b\), and $$\widehat{KL} = \max\left(0,\ \sum_b p_b \log(p_b B) - \frac{B - 1}{2\,ESS_P}\right),$$ where \(ESS_P = (\sum w)^2 / \sum w^2\) is the Kish effective sample size of weights1. The subtracted term is the leading finite-sample bias of the plug-in divergence of a \(B\)-cell histogram (the Miller-Madow correction), so an unmoved posterior scores about 0 rather than \((B - 1)/(2 ESS_P)\).

Percentiles. When samples1 and samples2 are the same draws (the posterior is a reweighting of the prior draws), the percentile of a draw is the midpoint of its cumulative Q-weight after ordering by value, ties in random order; with uniform weights2 this is (rank(x, ties.method = "random") - 0.5) / n. Otherwise it is the randomised probability integral transform against Q's weighted empirical CDF, \(u = F_Q(x^-) + U\,[F_Q(x) - F_Q(x^-)]\) with \(U \sim U(0, 1)\). Random tie-breaking spreads an integer-valued or point-mass parameter evenly over the percentiles its atom occupies.

Range. Binning can only lose information, so the estimate is at most \(\log B\) (3.0 nats at \(B = 20\)), reached when P falls into a single bin (1/\(B\) of Q's mass); it ranks parameters by how much they moved up to that ceiling. It is computed when \(ESS_P \ge B\); below that NA is returned with a warning. P-mass outside Q's range is counted in the outer bins. Near \(ESS_P = B\) the correction leaves a positive bias for an unmoved posterior (about 0.05 nats at \(ESS_P = 40\)), so MOSAIC reports the descriptive bands (.mosaic_kl_band()) only from \(ESS_P \ge 100\).

Before MOSAIC 1.4.0 both densities were weighted kernel density estimates integrated on a grid. That estimator failed for heavy-tailed priors (bandwidth set by the tail), integer-valued parameters (spikes) and priors bounded near the posterior (boundary bias), and was unbounded; values from the two estimators are not comparable.

Note that KL divergence is not symmetric: KL(P||Q) != KL(Q||P).

Examples

# Posterior as a reweighting of prior draws
set.seed(123)
prior <- rnorm(20000)
w <- dnorm(prior, mean = 0.5, sd = 0.5) / dnorm(prior)   # target N(0.5, 0.5^2)
calc_kl_divergence(prior, w, prior, NULL)
#> [1] 0.4366259
log(1 / 0.5) + (0.5^2 + 0.5^2) / 2 - 0.5                  # analytic KL
#> [1] 0.4431472

# Two separate samples
calc_kl_divergence(rnorm(5000, 1, 0.5), NULL, rnorm(5000), NULL)
#> [1] 0.7832714
